newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Hank Williams Jr. sees the father he never knew.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Hank Williams Jr. sees the father he never knew.

text.p: On Monday nights, he's the bearded guy who bellows on U.S. television sets across the country "Are you ready for some football?"

But on a recent, non-Monday Night Football evening, in dark glasses and a cowboy hat, Hank Williams Jr. is quiet and introspective, as he meets the ghost of a father the music world knew but he didn't.
"He changed a lot of the original words, didn't he?" muses Williams, leaning forward to stare at the scrawled lyrics of "Your Cheatin' Heart" on a yellowed manucript.

"That's what all good songwriters do. They put the words down first and then polish them up," he says of what may have been Hank Williams Sr.'s most enduring hit, now part of a new exhibit honouring his father at the Country Music Hall of Fame.
"That piece of paper generated a few dollars, didn't it," he added during a private pre-opening tour, looking at the words and phrases scratched out and replaced in his father's hand.
From the lobby outside comes the muffled sounds of music from Marty Stuart and Ricky Skaggs holding several hundred visitors at bay while Williams takes his tour.

Stuart, who donated many of the items on exhibit from his personal collection, was joining Skaggs on several Williams classics that still bring in royalties more than four decades since the star died at the age of 29 in a drug-induced stupor.

But away from the crowd it is the son, who lost a father at the age of three, who browses quietly, staring at the 1948 Packard that brought his father to Nashville for his first performance at the Grand Ole Opry.

The collection on display is somewhat amazing given its age and the carelessness with which the senior Williams left mementos strewn around. A newly discovered film of his 1952 performance on "The Kate Smith Evening Hour" is included.
There is also a computerized "scrapbook" that allows visitors to browse and play songs from a jukebox linked to each electronic page.
"How about the ears on that baby," Williams chuckles. "They're the Williams ears, all right," he says of a family photo of himself as an infant.

His father crawled into a car on New Year's Day 1953 and died. His drug excesses had cost him his job on the Grand Ole Opry a year earlier and his marriage was wrecked. He was down to second-rate road shows.

Not many years before the lanky Alabama-born honky-tonker with a gift for words with poetic emotion had burst on the scene with his "Drifting Cowboys" band. Among his hits were "Move It On Over," "I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry," "Lovesick Blues" and "Cold, Cold Heart."
Then he went into a tailspin of despair.

An old friend, the late Minnie Pearl, once recalled standing with a drunken Williams in the Wings of the Opry after he had sung his inspiring "I Saw the Light" as he moaned "But there ain't no light, Minnie -- there ain't no light."

For a time is seemed the son would repeat the sins of the father. The younger Williams began performing his father's songs at the age of eight but later moved onto a self-descructive road that almost killed him.
In 1975 he nearly died after a mountain climbing accident in Montana when a fall split his skull.
Today the shades and beard hide the jagged accident scars and Williams Jr. has turned his life around.

In 1987 he was named the Country Music Association's "Entertainer of the Year" for the first of two consecutive years. Since then he has racked up several Grammy nominations and his career appears solid and enduring.

"You know," he says of his father, "I still talk to him. I imagine what it would be like if he could come back now and see me. Every time I win an award, I say 'Hey, what about that Daddy?' And he winks at me. We get along fine."
Club Records will soon release an album featuring the voice of Williams Jr. with his young son Hank III, who made his debut recently at the Opry singing "Three," a song from the new album.
When he stepped on stage he wore his grandfather's necktie and one of his jackets. His father was standing encouragingly in the wings.
